text.title: Business Model Planning Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules binding the four frameworks this artefact carries: what makes a Four Actions grid value innovation rather than expensive differentiation, when a strategy canvas is comparable, what "fit" means in the Value Proposition Canvas, and the conditions under which each pricing model may be selected.

rule.statement: `blue_ocean` MUST contain at least one entry in BOTH `eliminate` and `create`. A grid populated only under `raise` and `create` is rejected and returned for rework.

rationale.source: Kim & Mauborgne, Blue Ocean Strategy — Four Actions Framework

rule.rationale: Value innovation is the simultaneous pursuit of differentiation and low cost; the eliminate/reduce side is what pays for the raise/create side. A grid that only adds raises the cost structure in step with the value proposition, so the offer needs a price premium — from buyers who were chosen precisely because they would not pay one.

rule.statement: The `strategy_canvas` MUST plot the incumbent curve and the proposed curve over an identical, identically ordered list of competing factors. Curves with different factor lists, or with factors that exist only on the proposed offer, are invalid.
rule.rationale: The canvas asserts something only through divergence between two lines on shared axes. Give each curve its own factors and the divergence is manufactured by the axis choice, so the picture shows a difference in what you chose to measure rather than a difference in strategy.

rule.statement: Every `pain_reliever` and `gain_creator` in `vpc.value_map` MUST cite the id of a specific pain or gain in `vpc.customer_profile`. Unreferenced value-map items are struck from the artefact, not carried as "nice to have".

rationale.source: Osterwalder et al., Value Proposition Design — problem-solution fit

rule.rationale: Fit is defined as the mapping itself, so an unreferenced reliever is by construction a claim with no demand behind it. Value maps written before or independently of the profile reliably produce a feature list that reads as a value proposition and then fails to move conversion.

rule.statement: Entries in `vpc.customer_profile.jobs` MUST be written as verb + object + circumstance ("file a quarterly VAT return for a client in another EU country before the deadline"). Role, industry or demographic labels ("freelancers in Portugal", "SMB marketers") are rejected as jobs.

rationale.source: Jobs-to-be-Done framing within the Value Proposition Canvas

rule.rationale: A role label does not constrain the solution — every competitor in the category serves the same role, so the profile discriminates nothing. Only the job plus its circumstance narrows the design space and identifies which alternative the buyer is actually choosing between.

rule.statement: `pricing_model` MUST name the unit charged, and that unit MUST increase as delivered value increases. `per-seat` is forbidden for products that remove seats from the buyer's workflow; `usage` requires a declared spend cap or forecast mechanism.

rationale.source: Value-metric selection in SaaS pricing and packaging practice

rule.rationale: Per-seat on an automation product prices the buyer's success as your revenue decline: the better it works, the fewer people they need logged in. Uncapped usage fails on the other side — procurement cannot approve a line item with no ceiling, so the deal stalls above a certain contract size.

rule.statement: `freemium` may be selected only if the artefact states the marginal cost per free user and either shows it near zero or declares a hard usage cap on the free tier.

rationale.source: Unit economics of free tiers with metered inference costs

rule.rationale: When the free path calls a metered model or other per-request infrastructure, each free user carries real COGS, so growth increases loss linearly and the free tier becomes the largest cost line before conversion economics have been established at all. Classic freemium assumes a marginal cost near zero; that assumption is the thing that must be checked, not inherited.

rule.statement: `rejection_reasons` MUST carry one entry for every pricing model in the enum that was not selected, each naming the specific constraint that ruled it out.
rule.rationale: A single-candidate result is a preference presented as a decision. Recording why each alternative loses is the only checkable evidence that alternatives were evaluated, and it is what makes the decision cheap to revisit when the constraint that killed an option (inference cost, buyer's headcount, procurement rules) later changes.
